Anticholinergic and Tricyclic Toxicity

anticholinergic toxidrome · tricyclic cardiotoxicity · bicarbonate, benzodiazepine, physostigmineIs the QRS wide, and is a tricyclic involved?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Drug script
Bottom line
  • Anticholinergic signs or any tricyclic overdose: an ECG (electrocardiogram) first; a QRS over 100 ms, a ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension calls for sodium bicarbonate
  • Agitation or seizures: a benzodiazepine. No haloperidol; no physostigmine once a tricyclic is involved
  • QRS width, not pupil size, bowel sounds or a drug level, predicts seizures and arrhythmia
What it is

Anticholinergic toxicity: muscarinic receptors blocked by one drug or several, often psychiatric medications

A tricyclic overdose adds sodium-channel cardiotoxicity, seizures and coma

Mechanism

Muscarinic block hot, dry, flushed skin big pupils ileus, urinary retention, delirium Anticholinergic toxidromeHot as a hare (fever), dry as a bone (no sweating), red as a beet (flushing), blind as a bat (big pupils), mad as a hatter (delirium)

Cardiac fast sodium channels blocked wide QRS ventricular arrhythmia

Alpha-1 block hypotension; gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABA-A) antagonism seizures

Culprits

Tricyclics: amitriptyline, imipramine, clomipramine and doxepin (tertiary, most anticholinergic); nortriptyline and desipramine (secondary, least)

First-generation antihistamines such as diphenhydramine; clozapine; phenothiazine and butyrophenone antipsychotics, haloperidol included

Used for

Tricyclics: depression after first-line drugs fail; obsessive-compulsive disorder (clomipramine); insomnia (doxepin); neuropathic pain and migraine (amitriptyline, nortriptyline); enuresis (imipramine)

Risks

Cardiotoxicity, the most common cause of death; convulsions and coma also occur (Tri-C); fatal at relatively low doses

Insights

Bicarbonate works on the sodium-channel block, not on drug removal: it raises the pH and the extracellular sodium

Physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, reverses anticholinergic toxicity, yet it is contraindicated in tricyclic poisoning because it can worsen cardiotoxicity

Tri-C
  • Convulsions – GABA-A antagonism
  • Coma – sedation and confusion, progressing to unresponsiveness
  • Cardiotoxicity – wide QRS; QT prolongation that can bring torsades de pointes; ventricular arrhythmia; hypotension
Adverse effects at usual doses, by receptortap to open
MuscarinicDry mouth, blurry vision, constipation, urinary retention, fast pulse, confusionStrongest with amitriptyline; tricyclics are relatively contraindicated in older adults
Alpha-1Orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, reflex tachycardiaFalls in older adults
Histamine H1Sedation, weight gain
ReuptakeSexual dysfunction, tremor, seizures; serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs, such as SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors)
Sodium channelQRS widening; ventricular tachycardia or fibrillationContraindicated with conduction disease
2Urgent risks
CardiotoxicityWide QRS, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension

If the QRS is over 100 ms, or arrhythmia or hypotension appears, choose IV sodium bicarbonate.

SeizuresOne or more convulsions after a tricyclic overdose

If a seizure occurs, choose a benzodiazepine.

Looks wellA normal early appearance can still progress to collapse, because absorption varies

If a tricyclic was taken, choose ECGs repeated and close monitoring.

Suicide attemptOverdose taken to attempt suicide

If the patient is medically stable and thinking clearly, choose assess suicide risk.

3Differential
Look-alikes, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Fever, confusion, unstable vital signs, lead-pipe rigidityBuilds over 1 to 3 days after a dopamine blocker is started or raised; rigid; normal tone makes it unlikely
Primary psychosis flareHallucinations in a patient on several psychiatric drugsAnticholinergic signs (big pupils, dry hot skin, fast pulse) mean toxicity; haloperidol can worsen it
Sweating, clonus, hyperreflexia, increased bowel soundsMinutes to hours after a serotonergic drug is added or raised; clonus
Seizure or postictal stateConfusion after a convulsionSeconds to minutes, typically abrupt; fever, hypertension and hallucinations point to anticholinergic toxicity
Fever, big pupils, fast pulse, agitationSweating; anticholinergic skin stays dry
New confusion, agitation or hallucinations on an anticholinergic drugAn anticholinergic drug in an older adult: dry, warm skin and big pupils point to the drug as the cause
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext move
Big pupils and quiet bowel after a tricyclicCommon anticholinergic effects with no prognostic valueFollow the QRS width
Normal muscle tone and reflexesNot neuroleptic malignant syndromeNo bromocriptine
Clonus or hyperreflexia with sweatingSerotonin syndrome
Agitated and hallucinating, with hot, dry, flushed skin and big pupilsAnticholinergic deliriumA benzodiazepine; no haloperidol
Diphenhydramine or another first-generation antihistamine an empty bottle of “sleep aids”Anticholinergic; some lengthen the QT intervalECG
Weeks of hard, infrequent stools on nightly diphenhydramine for sleep; otherwise wellA relatively common anticholinergic adverse effectDecrease or stop the diphenhydramine; constipation testing waits for that trial
Pause point
Agitation and fever on anticholinergic drugs Offered: haloperidol for the agitation, or bromocriptine for the fever Big pupils, dry skin and normal tone → Anticholinergic toxicity; the ECG comes first
7Treatment
1

FirstEvery patient

Supportive care: airway, breathing, circulation; IV fluids for hypotension
2

DecontaminateUnder 2 hours, airway protected

Activated charcoal
3

CardiotoxicityQRS over 100 ms, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension

IV sodium bicarbonate infusion

Not physostigmine

4

Agitation or seizuresAt any point

A benzodiazepine

Not haloperidol or a phenothiazine: they add anticholinergic effect

5

Antidote, with careSevere central and peripheral anticholinergic signs, no tricyclic

Physostigmine

Contraindicated with any sign of a tricyclic or a wide QRS, as it can worsen cardiotoxicity

8Follow-up
Prescribing a tricyclic safely
WhenCheckWhy
Before startingPotassium; an ECG if age 40 or older, cardiac symptoms, or a QT-prolonging drug such as methadoneLow potassium and QT prolongation add arrhythmia risk
Conduction or coronary artery diseaseConduction disease: do not use; coronary disease: avoidQT prolongation and arrhythmia
Epilepsy, angle-closure glaucoma, older agePrescribe cautiously, with close monitoringLower seizure threshold; pupil dilation; anticholinergic effects and falls
Suicide riskDispense a small supply, such as 1 weekFatal at relatively low doses
After an MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor)Wait 14 daysSerotonin syndrome risk
StoppingTaper over weeks to monthsAn abrupt stop brings cholinergic rebound: nausea, sweating, headache, insomnia
Practice
  1. 34-year-old woman confused 3 hours after her husband found empty pill bottles takes amitriptyline for migraine and diphenhydramine for sleep picking at the air; skin flushed and dry; pupils 7 mm T 38.6 °C · HR 132/min · normal muscle tone → Electrocardiogram → an anticholinergic toxidrome with a tricyclic on board: an ECG first, because a tricyclic may widen the QRS; haloperidol adds anticholinergic effect, and normal tone argues against neuroleptic malignant syndrome
  2. 52-year-old man found drowsy beside his nortriptyline, prescribed for neuropathic pain one generalized seizure in the ambulance pupils dilated; bowel sounds absent BP 94/58 mm Hg · HR 118/min · QRS 128 ms → QRS duration → in tricyclic poisoning the QRS width predicts seizures and ventricular arrhythmia; drug levels come late and do not track toxicity, and dilated pupils carry no prognostic value
  3. 19-year-old woman 1 hour after swallowing her mother's imipramine somnolent but protecting her airway; skin warm and dry ECG: QRS 140 ms, sinus tachycardia BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 126/min · glucose 104 mg/dL → Intravenous sodium bicarbonate → a QRS over 100 ms with hypotension in tricyclic poisoning calls for sodium bicarbonate; physostigmine is contraindicated because it can worsen cardiotoxicity, and a drug level does not guide treatment
  4. 45-year-old man agitated 1 hour after an intentional amitriptyline overdose pupils dilated; skin dry; no bowel sounds ECG: QRS 118 ms T 38.4 °C · BP 102/64 mm Hg · HR 128/min → Physostigmine → physostigmine is contraindicated once a tricyclic is involved, because it can worsen cardiotoxicity; the wide QRS calls for bicarbonate and the agitation for a benzodiazepine
  5. 23-year-old man agitated and hallucinating after eating jimsonweed seeds mumbling, picking at the air; pupils 8 mm; skin hot and dry took no medications; no seizures ECG: sinus tachycardia, QRS 88 ms → Physostigmine → severe central and peripheral anticholinergic toxicity with no tricyclic and a narrow QRS: physostigmine may be used; haloperidol may worsen anticholinergic toxicity, and bicarbonate is for a QRS over 100 ms
  6. 41-year-old man on clozapine, confused for 6 hours after a breakup skin hot, flushed and dry; pupils dilated; bladder distended bowel sounds absent; tone and reflexes normal; no clonus T 38.5 °C · HR 128/min → Anticholinergic toxicity → dry hot skin, big pupils, retention and a quiet bowel with normal tone: anticholinergic toxicity; serotonin syndrome brings sweating, clonus and hyperreflexia, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome lead-pipe rigidity
Pairs with Suspected Overdose or Toxidrome: which toxidrome, and the first tests. Antipsychotic Adverse Effects: neuroleptic malignant syndrome. SSRI Adverse Effects: serotonin syndrome. Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal: illicit drugs and alcohol.
Transferable rule

In anticholinergic toxicity get the ECG: a tricyclic may widen the QRS, and the QRS, not the pupils or a drug level, decides bicarbonate, and any sign of a tricyclic rules out physostigmine.
